To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

continuous infusion with a lower total daily dose of imipemem, compared to intermittent short-term infusion at standard dosages, results in a lower fT>MIC, but not in an improved survival of critically ill patients.

the probability of target attainment of imipenen by MIC was robust (>90% for 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations) for intermittent short-term infusion up to MICs between 1 and 2 mg/liters, but for continuous infusion up to MIC values of 2 to 3 mg/liters.
continuous infusion of imipenems with a reduced total daily dose compared to intermittent short-term infusion results in a lower probability of target attainment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the population pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modeling of continuous versus short-term infusion of imipenems.
the development of a new, more efficient and effective treatment regimen for the critically ill patients suffering from nosocomial pneumonia.
the development of new mathematical methods and their application to problems in biology and medicine.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the probability of target attainment is better with continuous infusion than with intermittent short-term infusion.

the pharmacokinetics of continuous infusion of imipenems are not different from those of the standard intermittent infusion regimen, but the pharmacodynamics of continuous infusion are superior to those of intermittent short-term infusional therapy.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the probability of target attainment of imipenen-cilastatin by MIC is robust up to 1 to 4 mg/Liter, and that a reduced dose of 1 gram of imipenemen-cilastatin administered continuously for three days may be a reasonable alternative to the standard regimen for critically ill patients, but that larger clinical trials are warranted to confirm these findings.
continuous infusion of imipenems is not superior to short-term intermittent infusions in critically ill patients with pneumonia, and the total dose should not be reduced.
continuous infusion of a reduced dose of beta-lactams may be a promising alternative for the treatment of critically ill patients with severe infections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of continuous infusion of imipenems is not a panacea for all infections.
continuous infusions are more likely to achieve target attainment for imipenem than intermittent infusions at the same total daily dose.

continuous infusions of imipenemem-cilastatin at a reduced dose may provide a superior probability of achieving target attainment compared to intermittent infusions at a higher dose, but this finding needs to be confirmed in larger clinical trials.
